Everything else was pretentious emotionally vapid slop. One of those movies that we get more and more of these days that I believe get praised solely on the merit of not being another blockbuster, tackling mental illness, having a relaxed pace, little to no plot, leaving things ambiguous. Ticks all the boxes that for a good portion of people is all that's required to automatically larp a movie for being an artistic misunderstood masterpiece.

Alrighty then. Aftersun... it's nothing much. Sure, it's tender a little psychological but there's not much worth digging into here. It's a solemn, minimal film; very few characters, brief interactions and a hazy, dream-like presentation. The whole thing plays out like a distant memory that, seemed happy once, but as you age, you see the sad undercurrents of it. Neat idea, but the execution was spacey and pretentious. Aftersun follows a recently divorced dad and his young daughter on vacation. He's depressed and doing his best to hide it from her. She is growing up, starting to feel attractions and is making real connections with other humans. As the vacation goes on, the daughter and father begin to relate to each other on a deeper level. That's it. Aftersun is good insofar as you relate to it. Most people my age on this site come from fucked up, divorced, miserable families so they have these decaying memories. They look back and realize when they started to realize the cracks. They remember discovering how flawed and broken their parents were; coming of age in a world of dysfunction. I can't really relate so this movie didn't have as much meaning for ol' D.W. The Rumsfelds have always been intact. For me, it was a plodding, gimmicky bore that should have just been a short film or something. I'll never forget the first time I saw my father cry... but that doesn't make this movie good. The characters were middling; mostly slates for the audience to project their sadness onto. Alot of the editing was stupid too, and only sometimes justified. I did like the cinematography and acting, though, Paul Mescal is promising and I have liked almost all of his theatrical performances thus far. Aftersun didn't hold much value for me. I felt like it wasted alot of time and tried to pull heartstrings. It had good focus and some intentionality but when all was said and done, I just kinda threw my hands up in frustration. Pithy abstraction, faux-cuteness, faint natalism, not for me. Two Mutzies and Odenkirk-grade singing

Words cannot fully describe just how disappointed I am that this film did not land for me. For the last sort of three to four years ‘ Aftersun’ has been talked about as one of the most successful directorial debuts ever, and in the same breath one of the most moving films of the decade yet, I’m utterly let down. There were only really a few scenes I was able to honestly resonate with and I don’t believe Charlotte Wells completely unlocks the deeply personal and stagnant emotionality she desires. Fairly dissatisfied with Paul Mescal’s performance in the film too, in fact I feel as though Frankie Corio even outperformed the then 26-year-old which is shocking. It also completely derailed any nuanced meaning for me because the way he acts is a causality and emotional anchor for Corio’s character, so for him to then not prevail in the role was an immediate disaster. I hope that this improves on rewatch, granted I give it a second chance, although I don’t see that being super likely.

“Que pensabas que harías hoy cuando tenias 11?” Aftersun es una película que tenia guardada hace bastante tiempo, gente variada me la recomendaba porque parecía ser un film bastante crudo en cuanto a la relación parental y en simples palabras tocaba el corazón y te hacia llorar… no me pasó. Me parece interesante y precioso en verdad como la imagen y la paleta de colores que se ocupa te transporta realmente a la pre-adolescencia/niñez que Sophie concierne, me sentí en todo momento como si yo también conectara con mi niño interior. Sin embargo, creo que espere en toda la película a que sucediera algo sorprendente o que turnara la trama a algo más denso, a algo que me deje nervioso, o sea si, se logra, sobre todo ad portas del final de la película cuando la relación entre Sophie y Calum parece quebrarse la noche de su cumpleaños, pero sin más, se me hizo demasiado pretensiosa y lenta, es una trama tierna y triste, sobre todo por Paul Mescal interpretando a este padre que parece estar depresivo. Acotar que, aunque se me hizo esperable el que no se volverían a ver, fue un sentimiento ingenuo de pena el que la película finalice con quizás los recuerdos de la mini cámara de Sophie sobre las mejores vacaciones de su vida. Quizás no entendí el film, quizás no es mi tipo de genero al cual recurro para disfrutar, realmente la quería disfrutar pero simplemente no me llego… Cerrando, me parece increíble leer los comentarios sobre esta película, muchos de ellos replanteando la relación que cada individuo tiene con sus padres, porque si, la trama te hace replantearte, de forma implícita, sobre todo aquellas personas con padres separados, y en un punto sentí, que los roles se invertían, el padre parecía un niño y la hija la madre, muchas de las realidades pasadas y contemporáneas, en donde los hijos deben ser adultos responsables a temprana edad (y quizás, solo quizás, por eso Sophie se nos muestra como una niña de 11 que intenta entender la vida [un tanto arriesgada, incontrolable y placentera de la mayoría de edad]).

This feels like one of those movies that is purposely vague in key ways to allow the audience to imprint onto it, and that kind of film is never going to work for me. At its core, we have a father and daughter on vacation together. There are moments where they bond. There is obvious childhood tragedy for the father, which is probably why he seems to drink a lot, yet he's not one of those abusive drunks, so it's ok? We're never really given much depth beyond that. It's a girl growing up, having a first kiss, hanging with other kids on vacation. It's nice that there isn't any kind of bullying or any other overtly negative elements that usually make up these narratives. It's mostly just moments shared between father and daughter, mostly bonding. At the same time, not much actually happens for the entire runtime. There seems to be implied longing, but again, the narrative is kept vague on purpose so that we can somehow imprint on it. The thing is, I am not watching a movie to do its job for it. If there isn't much story there, I'm not going to fill in the blanks for it. If I want to do that, I will either work on one of my own stories or read a book. Is this supposed to be sad and reflective? I never got to vacation with my father before he died when I was around 8 or 9, I never got these moments with him... and to have it be such a positive experience... this girl is fortunate. All I know is real tragedy related to my father. Did the girl's father die right after this? Or was it years later? We see her as an adult, all reflecting and shit, but as I said, things are left mostly vague, so who knows? At least she has cherished moments with her father. More than a lot of us got. On top of that, I think people confuse realism for good. Yeah, it is shot very realistically, the performances are very natural, yet story wise, there isn't much there, and I really dislike the way this was shot, which is probably one of the main sticking points for me. Often badly framed, or where it often focuses on 'experiencing', rather than what they are experiencing, so for instance, they are playing pool, we see them take the shot, but not any of what's actually happening in the game. Or another instance, they play an arcade game, but we never really see what they are playing. As for the bad framing, at times people are talking and the frame is like whatever. Or like, the scene where there is a TV, a mirror behind it, and the whole scene is either shot from a camcorder feeding to the TV or later, when the camcorder is off, what we barely see in the reflection on the screen or in the fragment of exposed mirror is all we get. It is certainly a choice. Oh, I get it, being so 'artistic' in its reflection on what's happening with the character, but it goes on for too long and it's just badly framed, all of it. Or this repeated cutting to a dance club, flashing lights, to show this reoccurring element of the father dancing... but mostly, it is just hard to see anything. Too much of the film is like this. Extended scenes of someone laying around, or badly framed shots like this that are clearly intended to be artistic, but end up being that in a bad way. I remember reading positive comments about this film and it sounds like it should be a good one, right? I expect a level of crudeness from a documentary, because it is trying to capture something in a moment and bring it all together, but when it's a narrative film that looks mostly like a badly shot documentary, that seems to have less story than many documentaries... what are we even doing here?

Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. Ok, so this took a lot of thinking, but I think I finally made sense of this film. This film made me see that you only know the version of someone that they show to you. The memories you have with or of someone are probably not actually what happened or who they truly are and felt in those moments. Our memories, especially from childhood can often have a rose coloured lense over them because at that time, you weren't aware of things in the grand scheme. You had an innocent mind because you were a kid. Most of my personal childhood memories have gaps. These gaps could have been good events or not so good events, and I'll never know because there was no camera. My siblings probably share the same memories as me, but with less or more gaps, with different details and specifics. My parents probably remember every specific and have no gaps in the memories I have from being a kid. Its like we were all there, at the same event, where we experienced the same thing, but we all probably remember it a little bit different. I probably won't remember writing this review, the same way I don't remember writing most of my reviews after a few weeks. Memory is a weird thing when you think about it. “You can live wherever you want to live. Be whoever you want to be. You have time." I used to envy people who had a documented life when they were kids, pictures and videos of them living as if it was the proof of existence. To see them through the eyes of their parents on how much they love and care enough to capture those moments, something to look back on in the future. I think it stems from my hatred and shame that every time there is an activity in school that requires baby photos, I will always be the only one worrying, for I have nothing to show. Maybe it was due to poverty? Lack of love and attention? Maybe they don’t just see the point in taking photos? Or maybe a little bit of a mix of all? It kinda felt bitter and pathetic, just a child wondering why I am the only one in the room who lacks that experience…and weirdly enough, I would find myself imagining that I am the one in other children's shoes, fantasizing about what it feels like to be in their family? Throughout the movie I just kept on thinking and reflecting about my relationship with my Papa. Initially I had this realization that I’ve never had anything that I could look back to; we barely had any pictures nor memories since we never went on vacations, went on a trip, or even simply went out. But I thought it would be an awesome thing to do so…I do think he deserves to have fun and do trivial things and see life without always being in a survival mode worrying about spending money on what seems to fit in the ‘wants’ and not ‘need’ category. I’ve spent most of my life with him, and I think personality-wise I am more like him. I might not like him as a person with some of his questionable morals and beliefs, but I could pretty much say that he was a great dad who literally did everything just so that me and my brother doesn't have to worry going on an empty stomach and even provide things that might not be grand, but it was better than having nothing. Actually, I do think that my dad is a cool person; he experienced so much hardship in life and knows a lot of skills in order to survive. I sometimes wish that I knew him better or even bonded with him with life outside of the house. Other times, I imagine what would his life be if I hadn't existed? The sole reason why I want to succeed in life, to have money, is just to spoil them and return all the hard work they've put in raising me; growing up, I think my parents value money more than anything, and I do get why, so I thought that maybe giving back with money would be the best thing they would totally appreciate—so that they could finally live the life for themselves and experience what they truly deserve: pampering their own needs and not for the sake of other people.

I sat down and watched this twice consecutively tonight. I think part of the beauty of this film is that it takes a minute to get. it’s very beautiful and visually impressive, but the deeper meaning is definitely supposed to be lost to you on your first viewing, seeing as the whole thing happens in Sophie’s imagination. you are living it through her as she tries to piece together her memories of the trip and who her father really was. the symbolism here is insane. there’s definitely more to unpack, but the two that stood out to me were the “rave” scenes being a metaphor for Sophie’s incomplete memories of Calum, and the polaroid photograph that sort of made the movie’s meaning click for me: that the physical media is really all Soph can see when she delves back into her old memories. on my first viewing I didn’t really get it until that moment - I just thought it was very pretty and was unsettled by how clearly disturbed Calum was on his own. but the second time around I cried. this is perfect and takes levels of understanding, which is exactly what I look for in a movie.

Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.
